rows.t: RWB App overview: what is the RWB app, what can it do, main screens and tabs
rows.k: features, sections, layout, where is, menu, bottom bar, navigation
rows.c:
The RWB App is the free app of Ronin Warriors of Bengal (on Google Play in India; iPhone riders use it in Safari at roninwb.in/app and can "Add to Home Screen").
Bottom bar: Home, Service, Mileage, Track (the big orange middle button), MotoMart, Warriors, Events.
Top right: calendar, ? (Guides), bell (news and alerts) and your photo (Me).
Pookie (the AI buddy) is the orange helmet button. Most of the app works offline and syncs when you're back online.

rows.t: Can live location be shared only with family members? Track privacy: who can see my location
rows.k: share location only family, private location, hide location from members, only my family see me, family only tracking, who sees me on track, location privacy, live location family
rows.c:
No. In the RWB App, Track has no "family only" option: while you share, every RWB member on the app can see you on the Track map, and members get a notice that you started riding.
Your RWB FAM (up to 3 family members you invite from Home → FAM) also see you live while you share. RWB FAM only ever see their own rider (plus riders on the same event ride), never the whole map.
If you want ONLY family to see you, don't share on Track; use WhatsApp or Google Maps live location with them instead. Stop sharing on Track any time: Track → Sharing live → Stop sharing.

rows.t: Track: how to share live location on a ride (Share, View, SOS)
rows.k: start sharing, live location, track button, go live, share ride, how long, until I stop
rows.c:
Tap the orange Track button in the middle of the bottom bar. You get three choices: Share, View and SOS.
Share: pick how long (1 hour, 4 hours, 8 hours or "Until I stop"). You can add a short note (up to 60 letters, e.g. "towards Simlipal!") that shows next to your name. If an RWB event ride is on, pick it under "Riding an RWB event?" (the app picks it for you if you're Going).
In the Android app sharing keeps running with the screen locked (a small notification shows). In a browser, keep the app open on the phone mount; locking the phone pauses sharing.
To stop: Track → Sharing live → Stop sharing.

rows.t: Track map: seeing riders, speed, follow a rider, directions, map styles
rows.k: view riders, map, where is everyone, rider speed, km/h, average speed, top speed, follow, directions, satellite, map style, full screen
rows.c:
Track → View shows everyone sharing right now. Pin ring colours: green = moving, amber = stopped, grey = no signal; the arrow shows direction and km/h shows on moving riders.
Tap a rider for: km/h now, average and top speed, km ridden this ride, how long they've shared, distance from you, Call, Directions (Google Maps) and Follow (the map keeps them in view).
Buttons on the map: full screen, map style (Street, Clean, Satellite), zoom, show everyone, and centre on me (tap again to follow yourself).
An event link (from the event page) highlights only that ride; other riders are dimmed under "Also riding now".

rows.t: Track ride lines: recent rides, ride replay, delete my ride line
rows.k: ride history, route replay, playback, recent rides, past ride, ride path, line, delete ride
rows.c:
After a ride shared on Track (1 km or more), a line of the route appears under "Recent rides" on the Track screen for 7 days, grouped by day and by event. Tap it to replay the ride on a map (play/pause, slider, speed up to 600×; event rides play every rider together).
Privacy: the part within about 300 m of the start and end of every line is never shown, so nobody sees where you live. Members see every ride; RWB FAM (family) can play back and save their own rider's rides and the event rides their rider was on, without top speed. You (or an admin) can delete your own line any time; lines are deleted automatically 7 days after the ride.

rows.t: Save a ride to my phone, keep a ride forever, top speed of a ride
rows.k: save ride, download ride, keep ride, saved rides, offline ride, ride gone after 7 days, top speed, highest speed, max speed, speed wrong, speedometer
rows.c:
In a ride's playback, tap the download button at the top right ("Save to phone"). The ride is kept inside the RWB app on your phone only (not on RWB's server), stays after the 7 days and plays even without internet. Saved rides are listed under "Saved on this phone" on the Track screen; tap the orange tick in playback to remove one. It stays on that phone only, so it's gone if you uninstall the app or clear its data.
Playback and Recent rides show each ride's top speed ("top km/h"). Top speed comes from the phone's GPS, which is the true speed; a bike's speedometer reads about 5–8% higher by law (it may never show less than the real speed), so 120 km/h on GPS is about 128 on the bike's speedometer. The phone sends its speed about every 5 seconds, so a very short burst can be missed.

rows.t: SOS in the RWB app: how to send an emergency alert
rows.k: emergency, accident, help, breakdown alert, danger, sos button, cancel sos, i'm safe
rows.c:
Track → SOS → press and HOLD the button for 2 seconds. Every RWB admin and coordinator gets an urgent alert with your location (it's hold-to-send so it can't go by accident).
The SOS screen also lists the RWB team with Call buttons. In real danger also call 112.
When you're OK, open SOS again and tap "Cancel SOS · I'm safe". Admins can mark it resolved. RWB FAM members can't send SOS.

rows.t: Track notifications: alert when a rider starts sharing
rows.k: notification track, riding live alert, turn off track alerts
rows.c:
When a rider starts a new ride on Track, members get "📍 <name> is riding live" (or "📍 <event> is live on Track" for an event ride, once per event every 3 hours). You never get your own.
Don't want these? Me → Notifications → turn off "Riders who start sharing on Track".

rows.t: The Track button spinning green ring
rows.k: green circle, track tab glowing, spinning ring, live indicator
rows.c: The green ring spinning around the middle Track button means someone in RWB is sharing live on Track right now. Tap Track → View to see who.

rows.t: Track battery and background tips (Android)
rows.k: battery drain, location stops, sharing paused, background location, phone locked, battery optimization
rows.c: In the RWB Android app, Track keeps sharing with the screen locked; allow location "all the time" if Android asks, and don't force-close the app. If sharing stops on its own, check that battery saver isn't restricting the RWB app (Settings → Apps → RWB → Battery → Unrestricted). In a browser, sharing pauses whenever you lock the phone or switch apps. For long rides keep the phone on a charger.

rows.t: RWB FAM: family members in the RWB app (invite, what they see, remove)
rows.k: family, add family, wife, husband, parents, mother, father, son, daughter, brother, sister, girlfriend, invite code, fam code, family circle, fam app
rows.c:
RWB FAM lets you add up to 3 family members. Home → FAM shows your invite code (like RWB-XXXX) with WhatsApp, SMS and Copy buttons.
They open the link (Android gets the app, iPhone uses the web app), tap Continue with Google with ANY Google account (they must remember which one), then on the "No Account Found!" screen tap the big Join RWB FAM button (right under Join RWB) and enter your code. There's a video showing every step: Guides → App → Invite your family.
They see: your live location when you share on Track (and riders on the same event ride), your odometer, RWB events, important announcements, members, the gallery and the VRN check.
Their Home is kept simple: Track <rider>, Message and Call their rider, and Call RWB Coordinator (a list of RWB coordinators and admins with WhatsApp and Call buttons). Events, Gallery, Important updates, Warriorboards, VRN check and Guides are in the menu behind the RWB logo (top left).
They can't see expenses, RSVPs, MotoMart, Service, Mileage or other riders' phone numbers, and can't share location or send SOS.
Remove someone any time from Home → FAM → Remove (they lose access at once). Family members can also switch RWB FAM off in their own Me screen.

rows.t: RWB FAM: I forgot which Google account I used
rows.k: fam login problem, family can't sign in, wrong account fam
rows.c: An RWB FAM member must sign in with the same Google account they used when joining. If they've forgotten it, only the RWB member who invited them can help: remove them in Home → FAM and send a fresh invite, then they join again with the account they want to keep.

rows.t: Home screen in the RWB app
rows.k: home page, dashboard, odometer dial, ride health, shortcuts, quick buttons
rows.c:
Home shows your bike at a glance: the odometer dial (tap it to type the km your bike shows; the ring fills as the next service comes closer), km/l average, fuel cost per km and service spend this year.
Below: My Ride (part wear), quick buttons (Add fuel, Log service, FAM, Sell gear, Documents), the next RWB event, birthdays, the VRN check, Latest from RWB, Fresh on MotoMart, the RWB Gallery strip and Explore (Teach Pookie, Maintenance guides, New accessories, roninwb.in).
Admins and coordinators also get their panel shortcuts on Home.

rows.t: How to update my odometer km in the app
rows.k: odometer, change km, wrong km, update kilometers, reading
rows.c: Tap the big kilometre number (the dial) on Home, type what your bike's odometer shows and tap Save. Adding a fill-up or a service with the odometer also updates it.

rows.t: My Ride: tracking parts wear (oil, chain, tyres, brake pads) and accessories
rows.k: parts tracker, wear parts, ride health, replace part, chain kit, brake pads due, my ride name
rows.c:
Home → My Ride lists wear parts: engine oil, oil filter, chain lube, tyres, brake pads, chain & sprockets, air filter, spark plug, brake fluid, battery, cables, clutch plates and fork oil.
Tap a part to set its brand, size, date and km fitted and expected life. Life figures come from the TVS Ronin manual where it gives one, else typical figures (you can change them). A bar shows how much life is used; red = past its life, "Nearly due" = soon.
When you change a part, open it → "I replaced it: start a new one" (the old one stays in history).
Accessories & mods: add crash guard, top rack, exhaust, aux lights etc. with cost. Rename your ride (e.g. "Black Pearl"); only you see the name.

rows.t: Service screen: how to log a service and bill
rows.k: add service, service history, service record, bill photo, service centre, free service, paid service, AMC, edit service, delete service
rows.c:
Tap Service at the bottom → "+ Add service". Date and km are filled in. Choose the type (Free, Paid, AMC, Repair, Self/DIY), pick or type the service centre, add what was done and the total cost, and attach the bill (photo, PDF or Word). Tap Save service.
Tap any service later to see it, view the bill, Edit or Delete. The card at the top shows when the next service is due.

rows.t: Next service due date: how the app works it out
rows.k: service reminder, next service, service due, when is my service
rows.c: The app follows the TVS Ronin service chart: 1st free at 750–1,000 km (or 30–45 days), 2nd free at about 6,000 km (6 months), 3rd free at about 12,000 km (12 months), then every 6,000 km or 6 months, whichever comes first. Log your last service so the dates are exact. The Calendar and a reminder notification also show it.

rows.t: Mileage screen: how to add fuel and how mileage is calculated
rows.k: add fuel, fill up, petrol log, kmpl, fuel log, mileage calculation, km per litre, full tank, DTE, range left, trip A, check badge, wrong mileage, unrealistic mileage
rows.c:
After EVERY fill (any amount, full tank or not) tap "+ Add fuel": litres, ₹ paid, odometer and date. Optional: "DTE before filling (km)" from your dash, "Trip A (km)" (reset it at every fill-up for the most exact distance) and "Full tank" if you filled till the nozzle clicked off. Trip A gives the exact distance; Full tank or DTE tell the app how much petrol you used.
The app follows the petrol in your tank: mileage = km since your last reading ÷ petrol used. With Full tank or DTE it knows the level (Ronin: fuel left ≈ 2 L + DTE ÷ the km per litre your dash uses, which the app learns), so even a part fill gets its own mileage at once (≈ when DTE is used) and counts in your average.
Without DTE/Full tank, a fill-up's mileage = km since your previous fill-up ÷ its litres; a part fill shows "Pending" and is joined with the next fill-up.
"Full tank" on a fill that can't reach the top makes the app ask "Full tank?" first (Yes / No, it was a part fill); older ones like that show "Check" until you open and save them. If Trip A and the odometer disagree, the app asks "Check the odometer"; when the odometer gives an impossible mileage but Trip A doesn't, Trip A is used (and the fill-up shows Check so you can fix the odometer).
Works for every bike in Me → My bikes: the app uses that bike's full tank capacity.
Fill-ups that don't add up (an odometer typo, a missed fill-up, more litres than the tank holds, mileage a bike can't do: a Ronin over 55 or under 25 km/l; over 50 counts only when 3 readings in a row are over 50) show "Check" and are left out until fixed.
Your average and the Mileage Warriorboard use the same readings and need at least 200 km of good readings. Typed something wrong? Tap the fill-up and fix it. Forgot to log a fill-up? Tap the fill-up marked Check or Pending → "+ Add a missed fill-up before this one", enter its litres and odometer, and the mileage sorts itself out.

rows.t: Mileage with more than one bike, and tank capacity
rows.k: second bike, multiple bikes, other bike mileage, tank capacity, non ronin mileage
rows.c:
With 2 or 3 bikes, pick the bike when adding fuel; each bike has its own mileage (chips at the top of Mileage). Only the main bike's fill-ups count as odometer readings and for the Mileage Warriorboard.
For non-Ronin bikes the app needs the full tank capacity: Me → My bikes → the bike → Full tank capacity. The Ronin's 14 L is known already.

rows.t: Calendar in the RWB app
rows.k: calendar, reminders, renewal dates, expiry reminder, add reminder, fastag
rows.c:
Tap the calendar button at the top (left of the ?). It shows RWB events plus your vehicle dates: document expiries, next service, My Ride parts due, logged services and fill-ups, and your own reminders.
Tap a day with a dot to see it. Tap Reminder to add your own (e.g. FASTag recharge). Reminders also come as notifications in the morning.

rows.t: Documents: keep DL, RC, PUC and insurance in the app
rows.k: documents, papers, driving licence, registration, pollution certificate, insurance copy, aadhaar, expiry
rows.c:
Home → Documents. Add Driving licence, RC, PUC and Insurance (photo of each page and the expiry date), plus any other document (Aadhaar, PAN, warranty, permits). PDFs and Word files up to 3 MB.
Only YOU can see your documents: not admins, not other members. The app warns you on Home before something expires.

rows.t: Events: RWB rides, joining a ride, I'm going, guests
rows.k: event, ride plan, rsvp, going, join ride, not going, guest, plus one, meetup, breakfast ride
rows.c:
Tap Events at the bottom: Upcoming and Past. Open a ride to see the date/time, place (Maps link), plan and who's going.
Tap "I'm going 🏍️" to join (everyone can see you joined); "Not going" takes you off. If the team allows it, switch on "Bringing a guest (+1)". If slots are full you'll see "Event full".
Use the calendar icon to add it to your phone's calendar. During the ride, the event page has "Share for this ride" (Track) and "See riders on map".

rows.t: Event expenses: split costs with the group
rows.k: expenses, split bill, who pays whom, money, cost sharing, settle up
rows.c: On an event page, the Expenses section lets people who are going add shared costs (e.g. breakfast ₹1,200). The app splits each expense only among those going and shows who pays whom. You must join the event to see and add expenses.

rows.t: Creating and managing events (admins and coordinators)
rows.k: create event, edit event, cancel event, add rider to event, share event card, going list
rows.c:
Admins and coordinators see "+ Create event" in Events (every member gets a notification). They can add a landscape cover photo, slots, guests on/off, a call link and a reminder.
On the event they can Edit, Cancel or Delete it, add or remove anyone from the Going list (even members not on the app), share a poster card with the share icon on the cover, and send the Going list to WhatsApp with "Share list".

rows.t: Warriors and Warriorboards (leaderboards)
rows.k: leaderboard, ranking, top riders, rank, warriorboard, hall of fame, track warriors, mileage warriors, road warriors, service warriors, pookie warriors
rows.c:
Tap Warriors at the bottom. Five boards: Track Warriors (km ridden while sharing on Track), Mileage Warriors (best average km/l of each rider's main bike), Service Warriors (services logged), Road Warriors (odometer km) and Pookie Warriors (XP from Teach Pookie).
Switch period with Week, Month, 3M, 6M, Year, All. Swipe or tap tiles to change board; your own rank shows on each tile.
Don't want to appear? Me → Privacy → turn off "Show me on the Warriorboards".

rows.t: RWB Members list: find a rider, team contacts
rows.k: member list, directory, find member, search rider, contact admin, members page
rows.c: Warriors → RWB Members lists every rider and the RWB team. Everyone in the app is shown by their first name (or their nickname, if they set one) and photo; other details (VRN, bike model, locality, mileage) show only if that rider shares them (Me → Privacy). Admins and coordinators can see full details.

rows.t: VRN check: is this bike's rider in RWB?
rows.k: number plate check, registration check, vrn, spotted a ronin, is he a member
rows.c: On Home, type a bike number in "VRN check" (e.g. WB 02 AB 1234) and tap Check. ✅ means the rider is an RWB member (name partly hidden for privacy, with their area); ❌ means not a member, so say hi politely and tell them about RWB or roninwb.in.

rows.t: Me: profile, edit details, photo, my bikes
rows.k: profile, edit profile, change name, change phone, change email, add bike, second bike, change photo, blood group, emergency contact
rows.c:
Tap your photo (top right) → Me. Change your photo with the camera icon. "Edit profile" changes your details; changes to Full Name, WhatsApp number, Email and main bike number are checked by an admin first, the rest saves at once.
My bikes: up to 3 bikes. Also here: notifications, privacy, theme (Light, Dark, Auto), WhatsApp app choice, Terms, Report a problem, Sign out and Delete my account.

rows.t: Changing my email or Google account in the RWB app
rows.k: change email, new google account, different gmail, email change
rows.c: Me → Edit profile → change the email. An admin approves it; then you're signed out of the old account and you sign in with the new Google account. Everything you saved moves across.

rows.t: Privacy settings: what other members can see about me
rows.k: privacy, hide my number, hide bike, hide locality, show mileage, data sharing, who sees my details
rows.c: Me → Privacy. Members see you by your first name (or nickname) and photo. Choose whether they also see: VRN and bike numbers, bike model, locality and average mileage ("Share all"/"Hide all" button too). Your phone number is not shown to members. RWB admins and coordinators can always see your details. Documents are private to you only.

rows.t: Notifications in the RWB app: turn on or off
rows.k: notifications, alerts, push, not getting notifications, turn off alerts, bell
rows.c:
Me → Notifications: turn notifications on for this phone and choose: renewal/service/my reminders, riders who start sharing on Track, riders joining events, new MotoMart posts, new members (admins also: birthdays). RWB announcements always come through.
Not getting any? Check Android Settings → Apps → RWB → Notifications are allowed, and that battery saver isn't blocking the app.
The bell (top right) shows news and alerts; swipe one to hide it, or Clear (admin announcements and events stay until removed).

rows.t: Dark mode / light mode in the app
rows.k: theme, dark theme, light theme, appearance, night mode
rows.c: Me → Appearance → Light, Dark or Auto (follows your phone).

rows.t: MotoMart: buy and sell bike gear, accessories and RWB merch
rows.k: motomart, buy, sell, marketplace, used parts, pre-owned, second hand gear, shop
rows.c:
MotoMart (bottom bar) has tabs All, New, Pre-owned and RWB Merch, round category buttons, search (top right) and sort.
Pre-owned = members selling their own gear: tap an item for photos and price, then message the seller on WhatsApp. New = new accessories picked by the RWB team ("Check product" opens the store; RWB doesn't sell them). RWB Merch = official RWB jerseys, stickers etc.: "Get now" opens the order form or link, else RWB's Instagram DM. "Coming Soon" items can't be ordered yet.

rows.t: How to sell something on MotoMart
rows.k: sell gear, post item, list item, sell helmet, sell accessory, mark sold, delete post
rows.c:
Tap "Sell gear" on Home or "+ Sell something" in MotoMart. Add clear photos, the name, category, condition and price, then "Send for approval". An admin or coordinator checks it (usually within a day); an admin's own post goes live at once.
Limits: 8 active posts and 5 new posts a day. When it's sold, mark it sold (it greys out and is deleted 15 days later). WhatsApp shares of a post hide your name and number; buyers contact you from inside the app.

rows.t: Guides: maintenance PDFs, riding tips and app how-to videos
rows.k: guides, help, question mark button, maintenance guide, pdf, how to videos, tutorials
rows.c:
Tap the ? at the top. Three categories: App (short how-to videos for the app), Maintenance (bike care PDFs, videos and pictures; opens first) and Ride (riding tips). Filters: All, Videos, PDFs, Pictures, plus search. Guides open inside the app.
Only the team posts guides (Bodhi: all three; admins: Maintenance and Ride; coordinators: Ride).

rows.t: Pookie: the RWB AI, daily question limit, photos, languages
rows.k: pookie, ai, chatbot, ask pookie, questions left, limit, new chat, bengali, hindi, photo question
rows.c:
Tap the orange Pookie button. Ask about Ronin care, gear, routes, RWB or the app, and keep the chat going with follow-ups. Pookie understands English, Bengali, Hindi, Banglish and Hinglish. You can attach a photo (📷).
Each member gets 20 questions a day ("questions left today" shows under the box); questions Pookie can't answer don't count. The chat is kept only on your phone; "New chat" clears it.
Pookie answers from what RWB warriors and admins taught it plus RWB's checked notes. If it doesn't know, the question goes to Teach Pookie as URGENT.

rows.t: Teach Pookie: answer questions and earn XP
rows.k: teach pookie, xp, levels, road guru, ronin sensei, urgent question, earn points
rows.c:
Home → Explore → Teach Pookie (or the chip in Pookie). Answer Pookie's questions from your own experience: brands, km, prices, steps, what worked. Admins or coordinators check each answer; you get +10 XP for every approved answer (2 XP while it waits). Admin answers go live at once.
URGENT questions are ones riders asked Pookie that it couldn't answer, so they help right away. Skip any you don't know. Top teachers show on the Pookie Warriorboard.

rows.t: Joining RWB: how to become a member, join form, approval
rows.k: join rwb, membership, how to join, register, application, apply, add warriors, new member, waiting approval
rows.c:
New riders join in the RWB App or at roninwb.in/join: sign in with Google and fill the short join form. An admin checks it, usually within a day. Your status screen shows Request sent, On hold (with a note) or Not approved (with a reason).
Every rider is welcome: Ronin owners, Ronin booked, planning to buy, or riding another bike. Questions before joining go to RWB's Instagram DM, never admins' numbers.
Riders without a Ronin also tell the admins why they'd like to join (for example, they know someone in RWB, or it's a special request). Riders on another bike give that bike's VRN, which an admin checks, the same as for Ronin owners. If something is missing, the status screen says "One more step" with an "Add it now" button.

rows.t: Sign-in problems in the RWB app
rows.k: can't login, sign in, google sign in, wrong account, not a member error, login issue
rows.c: Sign in with the Google account (Gmail) you used when joining RWB. If the app says you're not linked, use the short request form on that screen so an admin can link your account. If you changed your Gmail, ask for an email change (Me → Edit profile) from your old account, or tell an admin via the app's Report a problem.

rows.t: Delete my RWB account
rows.k: delete account, remove my data, leave app, deactivate
rows.c: Me → Delete my account. It deletes your RWB App account and what you added in the app. People whose join request isn't approved yet can use "Delete my request" on their status screen. roninwb.in/delete-account explains everything.

rows.t: Report a problem in the app
rows.k: report, complaint, bug, abuse, something wrong, feedback
rows.c: Me → Report a problem: tell the RWB team about anything wrong, unsafe or abusive in the app. Admins and coordinators answer reports, usually within a day. You can also report a MotoMart post from the post itself.

rows.t: RWB Gallery in the app
rows.k: photos, gallery, ride pictures, group photos, download photo
rows.c: Home has a rolling RWB Gallery strip; "See all" opens every photo, newest first (members and RWB FAM). Photos can't be downloaded or screenshotted in the app, to protect riders. Admins and coordinators add and delete photos.

rows.t: Offline use: does the RWB app work without internet?
rows.k: offline, no internet, no network, sync, changes waiting, hills no signal
rows.c: Yes, mostly. Screens you've opened before show from the phone, and fuel logs, services, reminders, ride parts and event RSVPs saved offline are kept and sent automatically when you're back online (a pill shows "Offline" or "N changes waiting"). Things that need live data (Track, MotoMart posting, Pookie) need internet.

rows.t: Installing or updating the RWB app (Android, iPhone, old APK)
rows.k: download app, install, play store, update app, iphone, ios, apk, old version
rows.c:
Android: get "RWB - Ronin Warriors of Bengal" from the Google Play Store (roninwb.in/get). If you had the old APK copy, the app will ask you to move to the Play Store version: open Play, uninstall the old app, install from Play. Updates come through Play; most screens update by themselves.
iPhone: open roninwb.in/app in Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen.

rows.t: Admin and Coordinator panels in the RWB app
rows.k: admin panel, coordinator panel, approvals, team tools, moderator
rows.c:
Admins get an Admin panel (Home → Admin → Open): Approvals (new join requests: New / On hold / Rejected), MotoMart (approve posts), Duplicates, Members (edit details, message), Birthdays, Reports, Pookie (check Teach Pookie answers, learn from Guides PDFs) and Guides.
Coordinators get a Coordinator panel: MotoMart, Pookie answers, Reports and Guides. Nobody approves their own MotoMart post except admins.

rows.t: Rate the RWB app
rows.k: rate us, review, play store rating
rows.c: Love the app? Rate it on the Google Play Store (the app shows a short "Rate Us" card in the Play version). It helps more riders find RWB.

rows.t: Who made the RWB app?
rows.k: developer, who built, app creator, tech team
rows.c: The RWB app is built and run by the RWB team; Bodhi, RWB's admin for tech, is the super admin behind the website, app and designs. It's free for every warrior.

rows.t: How do I set a nickname? How do I change the name shown in the app?
rows.k: nickname, display name, shown as, first name, change my name in the app, call me, name on track, name on warriorboard
rows.c: Me → Name in the app → "Shown as". Pick First name (the default) or Nickname and type it (2 to 20 letters). Everyone shows by first name unless they pick a nickname. Your chosen name shows on Home, Warriorboards, events and Going lists, the members list and notifications. The Track map, ride replays and WhatsApp messages from the RWB team always use your real first name. To change your full name itself, use Me → Edit profile (an admin checks it first).

rows.t: Yamaha XSR 155: specs, price, features
rows.k: xsr155, xsr 155, yamaha xsr, retro yamaha, xsr specs, xsr price
rows.c:
Yamaha XSR 155 (launched in India Nov 2025, about ₹1.50–1.59 lakh ex-showroom): 155 cc liquid-cooled single with VVA, the same engine family as the R15 and MT-15 (India spec about 18.4 PS and 14.2 Nm, revs to 10,000 rpm), 6-speed with assist & slipper clutch. Inverted (USD) fork, link-type monoshock, dual-channel ABS, 282 mm front / 220 mm rear discs.
137 kg, 810 mm seat, 10 L tank. Tyres: front 100/80-17 (MRF Zapper FX1), rear 140/70-17 radial (MRF Revz-S). LCD with Y-Connect app (call/SMS alerts, last parked location). Battery 12 V 4 Ah.

rows.t: Yamaha XSR 155 maintenance: service interval, oil, tyre pressure
rows.k: xsr service, xsr oil, xsr tyre pressure, xsr maintenance, yamalube
rows.c: XSR 155 service interval is short: about every 4,000 km or 4 months (Team-BHP review), so keep to it. Yamaha's 155 cc engines use Yamalube 10W-40 (JASO MA); the sump is small, so check the oil level regularly and don't stretch oil changes. Liquid-cooled: keep coolant between the marks. Yamaha's 155 cc platform usually runs about 29 psi front / 33 psi rear (cold); confirm on the sticker on your bike.

rows.t: Yamaha XSR 155: pros, cons and common complaints
rows.k: xsr problems, xsr issues, xsr cons, xsr review, xsr suspension stiff, xsr switchgear
rows.c:
Pros: gorgeous retro style, good fit and finish, rev-happy engine with good efficiency, roomy riding position, light and easy.
Cons owners mention: stiff R15/MT-15 suspension that's harsh on broken roads, budget-feeling switchgear with the horn and indicator buttons swapped (takes getting used to), short service interval, small 10 L tank, and not much low-end pull for a pillion and luggage on highways.

rows.t: Yamaha XSR 155 mods and accessories
rows.k: xsr mods, xsr cafe racer kit, xsr scrambler kit, xsr accessories, xsr crash guard
rows.c: Yamaha dealers offer a Cafe Racer kit (about ₹11,900) and a Scrambler kit (about ₹12,300), plus headlight guard, fly screen, bar-end mirrors, crash guards, radiator guard, adjustable levers and phone mounts (2025 prices). A radiator guard is worth it for broken roads. For touring add a tail bag and a tank bag, and plan fuel stops around the 10 L tank.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Himalayan 450: specs
rows.k: himalayan 450, new himalayan, sherpa 450, himalayan specs, himalayan 452
rows.c: RE Himalayan 450: 452 cc liquid-cooled DOHC "Sherpa" single, about 40 PS at 8,000 rpm and 40 Nm at 5,500 rpm, 6-speed with slip & assist clutch, ride-by-wire with Performance and Eco modes and switchable rear ABS. 17 L tank, about 196 kg kerb, seat 825–845 mm (low seat 805–825 mm), 21-inch front and 17-inch rear wheels: front 90/90-21, rear 140/80-17 (CEAT Gripp). Tripper round TFT dash with full Google Maps navigation.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 maintenance (RE owner's manual)
rows.k: himalayan 450 oil, himalayan 450 tyre pressure, himalayan coolant, himalayan service, himalayan chain slack
rows.c: RE manual (India): tyre pressure 32 psi front and rear, solo or with pillion. Engine oil 10W-40 API SN JASO MA2 semi-synthetic, about 2.1 L at an oil + filter change (check the sight glass; overfilling can affect the clutch). Coolant: ready-to-use RE-specified coolant (radiator about 815 ml at service + expansion tank to MAX). Brake fluid DOT 4 only. Spark plug gap 0.8–0.9 mm, battery 12 V 8 Ah. Chain free play 35–40 mm (long-travel suspension needs more slack). Clutch free play 9–11 mm. Running-in: under 6,000 rpm for the first 500 km. The service reminder asks for the 1st service early (about 450–500 km), then every 5,000 km.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 known issues and tips
rows.k: himalayan 450 problems, frame break, chassis crack, crash guard himalayan, himalayan issues
rows.c: In 2024 a couple of Himalayan 450 frames broke; both had aftermarket crash guards fitted. The engine is a stressed part of the frame, so RE recommends its own (GMA) crash guards: use RE's guard or one designed to mount the same way. Owners have also reported the bike pulling to one side and early software/dash glitches fixed by updates. Fill only to the bottom of the anti-splash plate. Low-fuel warning comes at about 3 L.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Himalayan 411 (old Himalayan): basics
rows.k: himalayan 411, old himalayan, bs4 himalayan, bs6 himalayan 411
rows.c: The older Himalayan (411 cc air/oil-cooled, about 24.3 PS and 32 Nm, 5-speed) was replaced by the Himalayan 450 in late 2023. RE manual: tyres 90/90-21 and 120/90-17; pressure 25 psi front / 32 psi rear solo, 27 / 34 psi with pillion; engine oil 15W-50 semi-synthetic (JASO MA2); tank 15 L. Known for comfort and toughness; owners complain about vibration at high revs, rust on the exhaust and spokes, and a cluster that can let in moisture.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450
rows.k: guerrilla 450, re guerrilla, guerilla
rows.c: RE Guerrilla 450: roadster on the Himalayan 450's 452 cc liquid-cooled engine (about 40 PS / 40 Nm), 6-speed, 17-inch alloys, 11 L tank, about 185 kg. Maintenance is very similar to the Himalayan 450 (10W-40 semi-synthetic oil, coolant, DOT 4). Check the manual or sticker for its tyre pressures.

rows.t: Royal Enfield 350s (Classic, Hunter, Meteor, Bullet, Goan Classic): engine and specs
rows.k: classic 350, hunter 350, meteor 350, bullet 350, goan classic, re 350, j series, royal enfield 350 specs
rows.c: The new-gen RE 350s share the 349 cc air-oil-cooled "J-series" single: about 20.2 PS and 27 Nm, 5-speed, smooth and torquey. Classic 350 (2021+): 19/18-inch spoked or alloy wheels (100/90-19, 120/80-18), 13 L tank. Hunter 350: 17-inch wheels, lightest of them (about 181 kg), 13 L. Meteor 350: cruiser, 15 L tank, 19/17 wheels. Bullet 350 (2023+) and Goan Classic 350 use the same engine.

rows.t: Royal Enfield Classic 350 / J-series maintenance (RE manual)
rows.k: classic 350 oil, classic 350 tyre pressure, hunter 350 service, re 350 oil change, 15w50, classic service interval
rows.c: RE Classic 350 (BS6 J-series) manual: tyre pressure 32 psi front and rear solo; with pillion 32 front, 36 rear. Engine oil 15W-50 API SL JASO MA2 semi-synthetic, about 1.7 L at an oil change. Services: 1st at about 500 km, 2nd at about 5,000 km, then every 5,000 km; the oil is replaced at the first service and then every 10,000 km (top up between; check level every 1,000 km). Chain free play 25–30 mm, clutch free play about 10–12 mm, spark plug gap 0.7–0.8 mm, battery 12 V 8 Ah, brake fluid DOT 4. Hunter and Meteor follow very similar schedules; check your sticker for their pressures.

rows.t: Royal Enfield 350 common issues and tips
rows.k: classic 350 problems, hunter problems, meteor problems, re issues, rust chrome, heat right leg
rows.c: J-series 350s are refined and reliable. Owners mention: heat on the right leg in traffic, rust on chrome/exhaust if not cared for (rinse and protect after rain), side-stand switch and fuel-gauge glitches on some units, and vibration only at the top of the rev range. RE's network is huge, so parts are easy to get. Older (UCE) 350s need more frequent oil changes and tappet checks.

rows.t: Royal Enfield 650 twins (Interceptor, Continental GT, Super Meteor, Shotgun, Bear)
rows.k: interceptor 650, continental gt, gt 650, super meteor 650, shotgun 650, bear 650, re 650
rows.c: RE's 650s use a 648 cc air-oil-cooled parallel twin (about 47 PS, 52 Nm, 6-speed, slip & assist clutch): smooth, relaxed highway cruisers. Use the RE-specified oil grade and follow the RE schedule; they are heavy (around 200–240 kg), so a good crash guard and care at slow speeds help.

rows.t: Jawa and Yezdi bikes: models and engines
rows.k: jawa 42, jawa 350, jawa perak, jawa bobber, 42 fj, yezdi roadster, yezdi scrambler, yezdi adventure, classic legends
rows.c: Jawa and Yezdi (Classic Legends) bikes use liquid-cooled DOHC singles with 6-speed gearboxes: about 294.7 cc (older Jawa 42, about 27 PS) and 334 cc (Jawa 350, 42 FJ, 42 Bobber, Perak, Yezdi Roadster/Scrambler/Adventure, about 29 PS). The Jawa 42 was updated in Sept 2026 with new bodywork and wider tyres. Tanks are about 12–14 L. Spec sites list about 23 psi front and 28 psi rear solo (30 rear with pillion) for the Jawa 42 family; confirm on your bike's sticker.

rows.t: Jawa / Yezdi maintenance and common problems
rows.k: jawa problems, jawa heating, jawa service, jawa oil, yezdi problems, jawa issues
rows.c: Owners commonly report: heat on the legs in traffic (the radiator fan running is normal), early electrical/ECU glitches, weak batteries, chrome rust, and patchy service centres. Tips from owners: service on time (many change oil every 3,000–5,000 km), keep coolant at the mark, spray WD-40 on chrome monthly against rust, increase rear preload to stop scraping on speed breakers, and keep the chain lubed. Oil capacity is about 1.25 L on the 42 family (check the manual for grade).

rows.t: KTM 390 Duke (2024+ third gen): specs and maintenance
rows.k: ktm 390, duke 390, 390 duke, ktm duke service, ktm oil, ktm tyre pressure, ktm 390 specs
rows.c: 2024+ KTM 390 Duke: 398.7 cc liquid-cooled single, about 46 PS and 39 Nm, 6-speed with quickshifter, ride modes, cornering ABS, traction control, about 165 kg (without fuel), 15 L tank. KTM specifies Motorex 15W-50 oil. KTM's manual service interval for the 398 cc bikes is 10,000 km or 12 months (the older 373 cc Duke was 7,500 km); many Indian owners change oil earlier in hot traffic. Valve check every 20,000 km. Check tyre pressures on the swingarm sticker (KTM road figures are around 29 psi).

rows.t: KTM 200 and 250 Duke, RC and 390 Adventure: basics and common issues
rows.k: duke 200, duke 250, rc 200, rc 390, 390 adventure, ktm problems, ktm heating
rows.c: Duke 200 (199.5 cc, about 25 PS), Duke 250 (about 31 PS) and 390 Duke share KTM's liquid-cooled, high-revving singles; RC models are faired, 390 Adventure (now X and R variants) is the touring/off-road one. Common owner notes: lots of heat in traffic (fan comes on a lot), firm seats, chain wears fast if not lubed, and service quality varies by dealer. Use 15W-50 (or the manual's grade) JASO MA2 oil, keep coolant topped up and the radiator clean.

rows.t: Honda CB350 H'ness / CB350RS / CB350
rows.k: honda cb350, hness, h'ness, cb350rs, honda bigwing
rows.c: Honda CB350 family: 348.36 cc air-cooled single, about 21 PS at 5,500 rpm and 30 Nm at 3,000 rpm, 5-speed with assist & slipper clutch, Honda Selectable Torque Control (traction control), dual-channel ABS, 15 L tank, about 181 kg (H'ness). Service about every 6,000 km (sold through Honda BigWing). Spec listings show about 29 psi front / 33 psi rear for the H'ness; check your sticker. Known for smoothness and reliability; uses a Honda-specified 10W-30 JASO MA oil (check the manual).

rows.t: Triumph Speed 400 and Scrambler 400 X
rows.k: triumph speed 400, scrambler 400x, triumph 400, speed t4, bajaj triumph
rows.c: Triumph Speed 400: 398.15 cc liquid-cooled DOHC single, about 40 PS at 8,000 rpm and 37.5 Nm at 6,500 rpm, 6-speed with slip & assist clutch, 43 mm USD fork, traction control, dual-channel ABS, 13 L tank, about 176 kg. Service interval is long: 16,000 km or 12 months (valve check at 32,000 km), with a 2-year unlimited-km warranty; sold and serviced through Bajaj-Triumph dealers. Lube the chain often (Triumph says every few hundred km), and many owners still change oil earlier in Indian traffic. The Speed T4 is the cheaper, simpler version.

rows.t: Hero Xpulse 210 and Xpulse 200 4V
rows.k: xpulse, xpulse 210, xpulse 200, hero adventure, xpulse service
rows.c:
Hero Xpulse 210 (2025): new 210 cc liquid-cooled DOHC single, about 24.6 PS and 20.7 Nm, 6-speed, 21-inch front / 18-inch rear spoked wheels (90/90-21, 120/80-18), 13 L tank, 168–170 kg, 220 mm ground clearance, 830 mm seat, ABS modes. Service: check-up at 1,000 km, then every 6,000 km or 6 months; warranty 5 years / 70,000 km. Spark plug Bosch VR5NEU (gap 1.0–1.1 mm); about 1.25 L oil at a drain without filter change.
The older Xpulse 200 4V uses a 199.6 cc oil-cooled engine (about 19 PS, 5-speed); great light off-roader with a cheap service network.

rows.t: TVS Apache RTR 310 and RR 310
rows.k: apache 310, rtr 310, rr 310, apache rtr 310 problems, tvs 310
rows.c: TVS Apache RTR 310: 312 cc reverse-inclined liquid-cooled single (about 35 PS), 6-speed with bidirectional quickshifter, ride modes, TFT with SmartXonnect, 11 L tank, about 169 kg; higher trims add tyre-pressure monitoring, adjustable suspension and a climate-controlled seat. The RR 310 is the faired sibling (BMW G310 engine family). Use the oil grade in the TVS manual and keep coolant topped up. Owners often report first paid services around ₹2,700 (oil, filter, washer, coolant top-up).

rows.t: TVS Apache RTR 160 4V and 200 4V
rows.k: apache 160, rtr 160 4v, apache 200, rtr 200 4v, apache fork oil
rows.c: Apache RTR 160 4V (159.7 cc, oil-cooled) and 200 4V (197.75 cc, oil-cooled) are light, sporty commuters with good TVS service coverage. Tip from a Team-BHP owner: the 160 4V manual specifies 240 ml of fork oil per fork leg, and some service centres under-fill; if the front feels harsh or bottoms out, ask them to check. Change oil and lube the chain on schedule.

rows.t: Bajaj Pulsar NS200, N250, Dominar 400 and 250
rows.k: pulsar ns200, pulsar n250, dominar 400, dominar 250, bajaj
rows.c: Pulsar NS200 (199.5 cc liquid-cooled, about 24.5 PS, 6-speed), Pulsar N250/F250 (249 cc oil-cooled), Dominar 250 (248.8 cc liquid-cooled, about 27 PS) and Dominar 400 (373 cc liquid-cooled, about 40 PS) are popular value bikes with a big Bajaj service network. Bajaj's Dominar 250 manual lists 25 psi front / about 28 psi rear solo; check your own sticker. Bajaj says all its bikes from the last 10 years are E20 compatible.

rows.t: Yamaha R15 V4 and MT-15 V2
rows.k: r15, r15 v4, mt15, mt-15, yamaha 155
rows.c: R15 V4 and MT-15 V2 use Yamaha's 155 cc liquid-cooled VVA engine (same family as the XSR 155): about 18.4 PS, 6-speed, assist & slipper clutch. Short service intervals, Yamalube 10W-40, about 29 psi front / 33 psi rear (Yamaha 155 platform; check the sticker). Sporty, light and efficient; harsh on bad roads.

rows.t: Harley-Davidson X440, Hero Mavrick 440, RE Scram 440
rows.k: x440, harley x440, mavrick 440, scram 440, 440cc
rows.c: Harley-Davidson X440 and Hero Mavrick 440 share a 440 cc air-oil-cooled long-stroke single (about 27 PS, strong low-end torque), built by Hero. RE Scram 440 is RE's 443 cc air-oil-cooled scrambler (replaced the Scram 411). All are relaxed, torquey highway bikes; follow the maker's oil grade and schedule.

rows.t: Choosing a bike to buy (any brand)
rows.k: which bike to buy, best bike, bike suggestion, first bike, budget bike, touring bike
rows.c: Decide what you'll mostly do (city, highway touring, broken roads, off-road), your height (seat height and weight), budget including insurance and service, and the service network near you. Test ride your shortlist back to back, ride with a pillion if you'll carry one, and talk to owners (RWB has riders of many bikes: ask in the group). For Bengal roads and touring, a light bike with good suspension, a comfy seat and an easy service network matters more than peak power.

rows.t: Engine oil grades explained: 10W-30, 10W-40, 15W-50, synthetic, JASO MA2
rows.k: oil grade meaning, viscosity, which oil, synthetic vs semi synthetic, mineral oil, jaso ma ma2, api sl sn
rows.c:
In "10W-30", 10W is how thin the oil is when cold (lower = flows faster at start-up) and 30 is its thickness when hot. Use the grade in YOUR bike's manual; a slightly thicker hot grade (e.g. 10W-40 instead of 10W-30) is a common choice in Indian heat, but don't go far off spec.
Fully synthetic lasts and protects best, semi-synthetic is in between, mineral is cheapest. For bikes with a wet clutch (almost all Indian bikes) the oil MUST say JASO MA or MA2; car oils and "energy conserving" oils can make the clutch slip. API SL/SN etc. is the quality level: use the manual's level or newer.

rows.t: How often to change engine oil
rows.k: oil change interval, when to change oil, oil change km, oil life
rows.c: Follow the manual's interval (it's usually given as km OR months, whichever comes first). Change sooner if you ride mostly in stop-go traffic, dust, heavy rain, very short trips, or flog it on highways in summer. Many riders in India change a bit earlier than the manual (e.g. at 4,000–5,500 km on 6,000 km intervals). Always change the oil filter with the oil, and replace the drain bolt washer.

rows.t: Checking engine oil level correctly
rows.k: check oil, dipstick, sight glass, oil level, low oil
rows.c: Bike upright (centre stand, or held straight if it only has a side stand), engine stopped for a few minutes. Dipstick bikes: wipe, insert as the manual says (many read with the dipstick resting, not screwed in), read between MIN and MAX. Sight-glass bikes: read the window with the bike upright. Don't overfill: too much oil can affect the clutch and seals.

rows.t: Tyre pressure basics: why it matters and how to check
rows.k: tyre pressure tips, check air, cold pressure, nitrogen, inflate, psi, tyre pressure for highway
rows.c:
Check pressure at least weekly and before long rides, with the tyres COLD, using your own gauge (petrol pump gauges are often off). Use the figures on the sticker (chain guard/swingarm) or manual; add the pillion/load figure when riding two-up or with luggage.
Low pressure = heavy steering, heat, more wear and worse mileage; too high = less grip, harsher ride. Nitrogen is optional; the right pressure matters far more than the gas.

rows.t: Tubeless tyre puncture: how to fix on the road
rows.k: puncture, flat tyre, tubeless repair, puncture kit, strip, inflator, nail in tyre
rows.c: Carry a tubeless puncture kit (reamer + rubber strips + glue) and a small inflator. Steps: find the nail (soapy water shows bubbles), pull it out, ream the hole, push a glued strip in with the needle until about 1 cm sticks out, pull the needle out, trim, inflate to the right pressure, recheck after 10 minutes. It's a road fix: get it checked at a tyre shop. Don't repair sidewall cuts or big gashes; replace that tyre. Spoked rims with tubes need a tube or patch kit instead.

rows.t: When to replace tyres: tread depth, age, cracks
rows.k: tyre life, worn tyre, tread, tyre age, dot code, tyre cracks, replace tyre
rows.c: Replace a tyre when the tread reaches the wear bars (little bumps in the grooves, about 1 mm left), if it has cuts, bulges or deep cracks, or at about 5–6 years old even with tread left (rubber hardens). The DOT code's last 4 digits show week and year made (e.g. 2324 = week 23 of 2024). In monsoon, more tread = more safety. Change brake-hard rear tyres earlier.

rows.t: Chain cleaning and lubing (any bike)
rows.k: chain lube, chain clean, chain maintenance, o-ring chain, x-ring, chain spray, wd40 chain
rows.c: Lube every 500–600 km (more often in rain), clean every 1,000–1,500 km. Use a proper chain cleaner or kerosene sparingly, a soft brush, dry it, then spray lube on the INSIDE of the warm chain while turning the wheel (bike on a stand, engine OFF, never with the engine running in gear). Wipe excess after 10–15 min so it doesn't fling. O-ring/X-ring chains: avoid petrol, harsh solvents and pressure-washing directly. Check slack as per your manual.

rows.t: Chain and sprocket replacement signs
rows.k: chain kit, sprocket worn, chain stretch, hooked teeth, chain noise
rows.c: Replace chain and both sprockets together when: the chain keeps going slack soon after adjustment, the adjusters are near their limit, links are stiff/kinked, you can pull the chain off the rear sprocket by more than half a tooth, or sprocket teeth look hooked or pointed. Replacing only the chain on worn sprockets wears the new chain fast.

rows.t: Brake pads: how to check and when to replace
rows.k: brake pad wear, brake squeal, spongy brake, pad thickness, sintered, organic
rows.c: Look at the pads through the caliper: replace when about 1.5–2 mm of pad material is left, or when you hear grinding. Squeal often means dusty pads (clean with brake cleaner), glazed pads or a dry caliper pin. A spongy lever means air or old fluid in the lines: bleed and change the fluid. New pads need 100–200 km of gentle bedding in. Sintered pads last longer and work better wet; organic are gentler on discs.

rows.t: Brake fluid: DOT 3, DOT 4 and when to change
rows.k: brake fluid change, dot 4, brake oil, spongy brakes, brake fluid colour
rows.c: Brake fluid absorbs water over time, which lowers its boiling point (brakes can fade on long descents). Change it every 2 years (or as your manual says), regardless of km. Use only the DOT type written on the reservoir cap; never mix DOT 5 (silicone) with DOT 3/4. Dark fluid = old fluid. Brake fluid damages paint: wipe spills immediately.

rows.t: Battery care: weak battery, not starting, long parking
rows.k: battery dead, battery drain, jump start, battery charger, voltage, bike not starting battery, battery life
rows.c: A healthy 12 V bike battery reads about 12.6 V or more at rest; below about 12.4 V it needs charging. Most last 2–4 years. If you park for weeks, ride it weekly or use a trickle charger/maintainer. Clicking but no crank = weak battery or loose terminal (clean and tighten). Extra accessories (aux lights, chargers) should be wired through a relay and fuse so they don't drain it. Push/bump starting works on most manual bikes with a little charge (2nd gear, clutch in, run, release).

rows.t: Air filter: when to clean or replace
rows.k: air filter, dusty ride, air cleaner, k&n, filter clean
rows.c: Paper air filters are replaced at the manual's interval (often 10,000–12,000 km) and much sooner after dusty or off-road riding; you can tap/blow out light dust from the inside, but don't wash paper filters. Washable foam/cotton filters (like K&N) are cleaned and re-oiled. A clogged filter cuts power and mileage.

rows.t: Spark plug: signs of a bad plug
rows.k: spark plug bad, misfire, hard start, plug colour, iridium plug
rows.c: Signs: hard starting, misfire, jerks, poor mileage. A healthy plug tip is light tan/grey; black and sooty = rich/too much idling; oily = oil burning; white = lean/overheating. Use the exact plug type in your manual (heat range matters). Iridium plugs last longer but aren't magic. Replace at the manual's interval.

rows.t: Coolant for liquid-cooled bikes
rows.k: coolant, radiator, overheating liquid cooled, coolant level, coolant change, fan
rows.c: Liquid-cooled bikes (KTM Duke/RC, Himalayan 450, Guerrilla, Jawa/Yezdi, XSR 155, Apache RTR 310, Speed 400, Xpulse 210 etc.) need the coolant between MIN and MAX in the reservoir, checked with a cold engine. Use the coolant type in the manual (most are ready-mixed; don't top up with plain tap water except in an emergency). Replace as the manual says (often every 2 years or so). The radiator fan running in traffic is normal; temperature warning = stop and let it cool.

rows.t: Washing a motorcycle safely
rows.k: washing bike, pressure wash, bike wash, cleaning, shampoo, polish
rows.c: Wash with a cool engine (wait about 30 min after riding), use bike/car shampoo, and avoid pressure-washing directly on the cluster, switches, spark plug cap, connectors, wheel bearings, chain and air-intake. Dry with a blower or cloth (under the seat too), then lube the chain. Wax or a quick-detailer protects paint; a little WD-40 on bare metal and chrome (not brakes or tyres) slows rust.

rows.t: Rust prevention, especially in monsoon and near the sea
rows.k: rust, corrosion, chrome rust, coastal ride digha, monsoon rust
rows.c: After rain or sea-side rides (Digha, Mandarmani, Puri), rinse off salt and mud, dry fully, lube the chain and spray a light anti-rust/WD-40 on chrome, bolts and spokes (never on brakes, discs or tyres). Park under cover. Touch up paint chips early.

rows.t: Monsoon riding: bike prep and riding tips
rows.k: rain riding, monsoon, wet roads, borsha, brishti, rain tips, waterlogged road
rows.c:
Prep: good tyres (enough tread), correct pressures, working lights and horn, chain lubed more often, brakes checked, a rain suit and an anti-fog visor or pinlock.
Riding: slow down and double your following distance; brake gently with both brakes, early and in a straight line; avoid painted lines, metal covers, oil patches and puddles hiding potholes; cross waterlogged stretches slowly in 1st/2nd at steady throttle, never deeper than the exhaust or air intake. Use the bike's rain mode if it has one. After deep water, dry the brakes by gentle braking.

rows.t: Riding through water: engine stopped in water (hydrolock)
rows.k: water logging, flood, engine stopped water, hydrolock, water in engine
rows.c: If the engine dies in deep water, DON'T try to restart it: water may have entered the engine through the air intake or exhaust, and cranking can bend parts (hydrolock). Push it out, call the service centre or roadside assistance. Milky engine oil = water inside: don't ride. Insurance "engine protect" add-ons cover this kind of damage.

rows.t: Long ride / touring checklist (pre-ride checks)
rows.k: pre ride check, before long ride, touring checklist, trip preparation, inspection
rows.c: Before a long ride: tyre pressure and condition, chain slack and lube, brake pads and fluid, engine oil level, lights/horn/indicators, clutch and throttle cables, loose bolts (number plate, mirrors, crash guard), battery, papers (DL, RC, insurance, PUC) and fuel. Carry: puncture kit + inflator, basic tools, fuses, spare clutch/throttle cable on far trips, zip ties, tape, chain lube, first aid, rain gear and power bank. Share your ride on RWB Track.

rows.t: Toolkit to carry on rides
rows.k: toolkit, tools, what to carry, spare parts trip, emergency kit
rows.c: Basic kit: tubeless puncture kit, mini inflator, combination spanners/sockets for your bike's sizes, Allen keys, screwdrivers, pliers, spare fuses, zip ties, insulation tape, a little chain lube, rag, torch. On far trips add: clutch and throttle cables, spark plug and plug spanner, brake pads, bulbs/relays if your bike uses them, tow rope and a jump starter. RWB's "Parts to carry during long rides" guide in the app (Guides → Maintenance) has a full list.

rows.t: Fuel: normal vs premium petrol, E20 ethanol petrol
rows.k: premium petrol, power petrol, speed petrol, xp95, octane, e20, ethanol, fuel quality, mileage drop
rows.c:
Since April 2025, E20 petrol (20% ethanol) is the normal petrol at Indian pumps. Bikes made from about April 2023 are built for it (Royal Enfield says its BS6 bikes are E20-compliant since 2020; Bajaj says its bikes from the last 10 years are, including KTM). Government/ARAI tests say mileage can drop about 2–6%; some riders report more. Older bikes may need rubber fuel parts changed over time.
Premium (higher-octane) petrol only helps engines designed for it (high compression); for most commuter and 200–400 cc bikes, normal petrol of the right type is fine. Fill from busy, reputed pumps; you can ask to see the density check.

rows.t: Fuel additives: are they good?
rows.k: fuel additive, octane booster, injector cleaner, o2 sensor
rows.c: Mostly not needed with good petrol. If you use one, pick a quality one labelled "oxygen-sensor safe" (PEA-based) and don't overuse it: cheap additives with lead, silicone or manganese can damage the O2 sensor. RWB's guide suggests at most about every 3,000 km (or every 5–6 full tanks).

rows.t: Improving mileage on any bike
rows.k: better mileage, save fuel, fuel economy tips, increase kmpl
rows.c: Smooth throttle and early upshifts, steady 50–70 km/h in top gear where possible, correct tyre pressure, clean and lubed chain with the right slack, fresh oil, clean air filter and good plug, less idling, less weight and no dragging brakes. Track every fill in the RWB app's Mileage screen to see what helps.

rows.t: Riding a new bike: break-in for any motorcycle
rows.k: running in, break in, new bike first service
rows.c: Follow your manual's running-in rules (usually low revs/speed for the first 500–1,000 km, varying speed, no full throttle, no long idling) and do the first service on time: it removes early metal particles with the first oil change and re-tightens everything.

rows.t: Clutch slipping, hard clutch, or bike creeping in neutral
rows.k: clutch slip, clutch hard, clutch drag, creeping, clutch plates
rows.c: Slipping (revs rise, bike doesn't speed up) = too little free play, worn plates, or wrong oil (non-JASO MA). Dragging (bike creeps with clutch pulled, hard to find neutral) = too much free play, old oil or cable issues. Set the free play to the manual figure first, use the right oil, then check plates.

rows.t: Engine overheating warning signs
rows.k: overheat, temperature light, boiling, coolant warning, engine too hot, smell
rows.c: Stop safely if you see the temperature/oil warning, smell burning oil, see steam/smoke, or power drops. Let it cool with the engine off (don't open a hot radiator cap). Check oil (and coolant on liquid-cooled bikes), fan working, radiator not blocked by mud, and chain/brakes not dragging. Don't keep riding an overheating engine.

rows.t: Warning lights on the dashboard: what to do
rows.k: warning light, engine light, mil, abs light, oil light, battery light, check engine
rows.c: Engine/MIL light staying on = fault stored: ride gently to a service centre and get it scanned. Oil pressure light = stop at once and check oil. ABS light staying on after moving = ABS not working: brake gently. Battery/charging light = charging problem: switch off accessories and get it checked. Temperature light = stop and cool down. Lights that blink briefly at start-up are just self-checks.

rows.t: Storing a bike for weeks (parking long time)
rows.k: long parking, storage, not riding for month, bike stored
rows.c: Fill the tank (less condensation), clean and lube the chain, inflate tyres a bit above normal or use a stand, disconnect the battery or keep it on a maintainer, cover the bike, and plug the exhaust against insects. Before riding again: check tyres, brakes, battery, oil and that nothing nested in the air box.

rows.t: Service centre tips: avoid overcharging
rows.k: service centre tips, overcharged, job card, unnecessary parts, service bill
rows.c: Write down your issues and give them on the job card, ask for an estimate before work, ask them to call before replacing anything extra, ask for old parts back, check the bill line by line, and keep every bill (log it in the RWB app's Service screen). Buy consumables like chain lube yourself if they charge too much. Be polite but firm about anything not in the manual's schedule.

rows.t: Insurance for motorcycles: add-ons worth taking
rows.k: insurance renewal, zero depreciation, add ons, comprehensive insurance, third party, claim
rows.c: Third-party insurance is the legal minimum; comprehensive (own damage) covers your bike. RWB's insurance guide recommends these add-ons: zero/nil depreciation, return to invoice, rim and tyre protection, and engine and gearbox protection (water/flood damage). Roadside assistance and personal accident cover are also useful. Renew before expiry to keep your no-claim bonus.

rows.t: Group ride rules and etiquette (RWB rides)
rows.k: group ride, first ride with rwb, formation, lead, sweep, marshal, staggered, ride rules
rows.c: On RWB group rides: reach the meeting point on time with a full tank, follow the ride lead and never overtake them, the sweep (last rider) stays at the back so nobody gets left behind, marshals guide at turns. Ride in a staggered line on highways with a safe gap, single file on narrow or twisty roads. Keep your place in the line, signal early, no stunts or racing, keep the rider behind in your mirror at turns. Share your location on RWB Track (pick the event) so the team can see everyone.

rows.t: Riding gear: helmet standards (ISI, DOT, ECE) and what to buy
rows.k: helmet, isi, bis, ece, dot, full face, helmet brand, riding gear, budget gear
rows.c: In India a BIS (ISI-marked) helmet is the legal minimum; ECE 22.06 or DOT certification on top of ISI is a good sign of quality. Choose a full-face helmet that fits snugly (no wobble, cheeks pressed), with a clear visor and pinlock for rain. Then a CE-level jacket with armour (L1/L2), gloves, riding pants with knee armour and over-ankle boots. RWB riders' rough minimum budget: helmet around ₹5k, jacket around ₹6k, plus gloves, pants and boots.

rows.t: Night riding on highways
rows.k: night riding, dark highway, headlight, fog light, dipper, trucks at night
rows.c: Ride slower than by day, use high beam only when nothing is coming and dip early for oncoming traffic, wear reflective gear, keep a clean visor (scratched visors flare), watch for unlit trucks, tractors, animals and potholes, take breaks every 1–1.5 hours, have tea/coffee, and avoid heavy meals before riding. Aux lights must point down so they don't blind others.

rows.t: Riding with a pillion
rows.k: pillion, passenger, riding two up, pillion tips, back seat
rows.c: Raise the rear tyre pressure (and rear preload if adjustable) as the manual says for a pillion. Ask the pillion to sit close, hold your waist or the grab rail, keep feet on the pegs, lean with the bike and not move suddenly. Brake earlier and smoother, accelerate gently, and go slower over bad roads. The pillion must also wear a helmet (it's the law).

rows.t: Braking correctly and ABS
rows.k: how to brake, front brake, rear brake, emergency braking, skid, abs tips
rows.c: The front brake does most of the stopping (about 70%). Use both brakes together, squeeze progressively (don't grab), and brake mostly in a straight line before a turn. With ABS, in an emergency squeeze hard and keep it on; ABS stops the wheels locking. Without ABS, ease off if a wheel locks and reapply. On wet or gravel roads, be gentler and leave more distance.

rows.t: Cornering basics
rows.k: cornering, turning, bends, ghats, hairpin, lean, counter steering
rows.c: Slow down before the bend (finish braking while upright), look through the turn to where you want to go, keep a steady or slightly rising throttle through it, and lean with the bike. A light push on the inside handlebar makes the bike lean (counter-steering). On ghats and hairpins use a lower gear, stay in your lane, and avoid gravel and wet leaves at the apex.

rows.t: Riding in hills: Darjeeling, Sikkim, ghats
rows.k: hill riding, mountain, uphill, downhill, ghat road, engine braking, sikkim, darjeeling
rows.c: Uphill: lower gear early, steady throttle, don't ride the clutch. Downhill: use engine braking (stay in a low gear) and brake gently in short bursts so the brakes don't overheat. Honk at blind corners, stay left, give way to uphill traffic on narrow roads and expect landslide debris, wet patches and fog. Check brakes and pads before a hill trip.

rows.t: High altitude riding: Ladakh, Spiti, North Sikkim
rows.k: high altitude, ladakh, spiti, nathu la, ams, mountain sickness, oxygen, cold start altitude
rows.c: Bikes lose power at altitude (thinner air) and fuel-injected bikes adjust automatically. Cold mornings can make starting slower: let the battery recover between cranks. For you: acclimatise slowly, drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol, and descend if you get bad headache, breathlessness or confusion (AMS). Many border/protected areas need permits or fees (e.g. parts of Sikkim and Ladakh): check the official government portals before you go, carry ID copies, and fill fuel whenever you can.

rows.t: Highway cruising and long-distance comfort
rows.k: highway, cruising speed, long ride comfort, saddle sore, fatigue, ride all day
rows.c: Cruise where the engine feels relaxed (for small singles that's usually 70–90 km/h), take a 10–15 min break every 1–1.5 hours, stay hydrated, wear earplugs against wind noise, and stand on the pegs briefly to rest your back. A gel/air seat cushion helps on long days. Stop riding when tired: fatigue causes more crashes than speed.

rows.t: Accident: what to do (first steps)
rows.k: accident, crash, fell, injury, someone hurt, first aid, emergency number
rows.c: Make the spot safe (hazard lights, warn traffic), call 112 for police/ambulance if anyone is hurt, don't remove an injured rider's helmet unless they can't breathe, don't move them unless there's danger. Send SOS in the RWB app so the RWB team gets your location. Take photos, note vehicle numbers and witness contacts, and inform your insurer quickly. Good Samaritans helping accident victims are legally protected in India.

rows.t: Traffic rules and fines: documents to carry
rows.k: documents to carry, dl rc puc insurance, digilocker, mparivahan, traffic police, challan
rows.c: Carry (or keep in DigiLocker/mParivahan, which are legally valid): driving licence, RC, valid insurance and PUC. Both rider and pillion must wear helmets. Check pending challans on the official Parivahan e-challan site. Keep copies of your documents in the RWB app's Documents screen.

rows.t: Are loud exhausts, aux lights and fancy number plates legal?
rows.k: legal mods, illegal modification, loud exhaust, silencer, aux light legal, fancy number plate, hsrp, modified bike
rows.c: Loud aftermarket exhausts and removing the catalytic converter or silencer are illegal (noise and emission rules) and can be fined or the bike seized. Number plates must be the standard HSRP; fancy fonts are fined. Aux/fog lights are a grey area: keep them low, aimed down, not blinding, and switch them off in the city. RWB doesn't support illegal mods.

rows.t: PUC and insurance renewal
rows.k: puc renewal, pollution certificate, insurance expiry, renew online
rows.c: Renew PUC and insurance before they expire (riding without them can be fined). PUC is done at any authorised pollution testing centre (many petrol pumps); insurance can be renewed online by comparing quotes. Add the new expiry dates in the RWB app (Home → Documents) and it will remind you next time.

rows.t: Rain gear and staying dry
rows.k: rain suit, raincoat, waterproof, rain cover, waterproof boots, gloves rain
rows.c: A two-piece rain suit over your riding gear, waterproof gloves (or a spare dry pair), shoe covers or waterproof boots, a rain cover for the tank/tail bag, zip-lock bags for phone and papers, and an anti-fog visor (pinlock) or anti-fog spray. Bright or reflective rain gear helps others see you.

rows.t: Phone mount vs navigation screen
rows.k: mobile holder, phone mount, camera damage, ois, navigation, carplay, android auto
rows.c: Phone mounts are cheap and handy, but engine vibration can damage phone camera stabilisation (OIS) even with dampers, and phones overheat in the sun. A dedicated bike navigation screen (Android Auto/CarPlay) is safer for the phone and easier to see, but costs more and needs proper wiring. RWB's guide "Mobile Phone Holders or Navigation Screens" in Guides compares them.

rows.t: Intercoms for riding
rows.k: intercom, bluetooth intercom, communication device, bluarmor, helmet communication
rows.c: RWB primarily prefers Bluarmor intercoms for group rides. Look at range, battery life, rain resistance and whether it pairs with your friends' units. Keep volume reasonable so you still hear traffic.

rows.t: TVS Ronin 225 specifications: engine, power, torque, weight, seat height
rows.k: specs, cc, bhp, ps, nm, kerb weight, ground clearance, top speed, gears, dimensions
rows.c:
TVS Ronin 225: 225.9 cc single cylinder, 4-valve SOHC, oil-cooled, fuel injected. 20.4 PS (about 20.1 bhp) at 7,750 rpm and 19.93 Nm at 3,750 rpm. 5-speed gearbox with assist & slipper clutch. Bore × stroke 66 × 66 mm.
Kerb weight 159 kg (single-channel ABS) / 160 kg (dual-channel), seat 795 mm, ground clearance 181 mm, wheelbase 1,357 mm, tank 14 L. TVS quotes a top speed of 120 km/h in 5th. Idle (warm): about 1,300 rpm. Launched July 2022.

rows.t: Ronin variants 2026: Base, Base+, Mid, Top, price and features
rows.k: variant, which variant, price, ex-showroom, dual channel abs, traction control, smartxonnect, bluetooth, special edition, agonda, nimbus grey
rows.c: 2026 Ronin line-up (ex-showroom Delhi, Sept 2026, roughly): Base about ₹1.30 lakh (single-channel ABS, all-LED, Rain & Urban modes); Base+ about ₹1.42 lakh (cheapest with dual-channel ABS); Mid about ₹1.51 lakh (SmartXonnect Bluetooth: turn-by-turn navigation, call alerts via the TVS Connect app; Type-C charger; gold USD fork); Top about ₹1.63 lakh (adds traction control, premium seat, adjustable levers). Special colours/editions (like Agonda, Nimbus Grey) come and go. Prices change: always check with a TVS dealer for the on-road price in your city.

rows.t: Ronin tyre size and tyre pressure (TVS manual)
rows.k: tyre pressure, psi, air pressure, tyre size, front tyre, rear tyre, 110/70, 130/70, pillion pressure, hawa
rows.c:
TVS Ronin tyres: front 110/70-17, rear 130/70-17, tubeless, on 17-inch alloys.
TVS manual pressures (cold): front 25 psi (solo and with pillion); rear 28 psi solo and 32 psi with a pillion/luggage.
Check pressures cold (before riding or after the bike has stood a while); a hot tyre reads 2–4 psi higher. Many RWB riders run a little more at the rear (30–33 psi) on highways or loaded; never go above what the tyre sidewall allows.

rows.t: Ronin engine oil grade and quantity
rows.k: engine oil, oil capacity, how much oil, 10w30, oil grade, tru4, synthetic, jaso, 1.3 litre, oil change
rows.c:
TVS manual: TVS TRU4 Fully Synthetic SAE 10W-30, API SL, JASO MA2. Quantity at a regular oil change: 1,300 ml (1.3 L); after an engine overhaul 1,500 ml.
Change the oil and oil filter at every service (every 6,000 km or 6 months after the free services, whichever comes first), and clean the oil strainer. Any good 10W-30 (or 10W-40) fully synthetic with JASO MA2 works; JASO MA2 matters because the Ronin has a wet clutch. Check the level on the centre stand with a cool engine, dipstick wiped and rested on the threads unless the manual says screw it in.

rows.t: Ronin service schedule (TVS owner's manual)
rows.k: service interval, free service, first service, second service, third service, maintenance chart, 6000 km
rows.c:
TVS Ronin service chart (whichever comes first):
- 1st free: 750–1,000 km or 30–45 days (oil + oil filter, strainer clean, tappet check)
- 2nd free: 5,500–6,000 km or 6 months
- 3rd free: 11,500–12,000 km or 12 months (also spark plug + air filter)
- Then every 6,000 km or 6 months: oil + oil filter, strainer clean, tappet check, chain clean/lube/adjust.
Spark plug and air filter: every 12,000 km (air filter sooner in dust). Brake fluid: check every service, replace every 21,000 km or 2 years. Front fork oil: 36,000 km, if needed. Free services cover labour; oil, filters and parts are paid.

rows.t: Ronin running-in (break-in) rules for a new bike
rows.k: running in, break in, new bike, first 1000 km, new ronin tips
rows.c: TVS manual: keep under 50 km/h for the first 1,000 km and keep varying the engine speed (no long constant speed, no full-throttle bursts). The 1st free service at 750–1,000 km (oil change included) is the most important one; don't skip it.

rows.t: Ronin chain slack, chain lube and chain care
rows.k: chain slack, chain adjustment, chain tension, chain lube, chain cleaning, loose chain, tight chain, 20-25 mm
rows.c:
TVS manual: drive chain slack 20–25 mm (checked on the centre stand, in neutral, midway between the sprockets on the lower run). Lube about every 500 km (TVS suggests TRU SPRAY or TRU4 oil), and after riding in rain or washing. Clean it with a chain cleaner (not petrol/diesel) and a brush, let it dry, then lube the inside of the chain on a warm chain and wipe off extra after 10–15 minutes.
A too-tight chain makes a rattle/whine and wears sprockets and bearings fast; too loose can jump. Clean and adjust at every service.

rows.t: Ronin clutch free play and clutch cable
rows.k: clutch play, clutch adjustment, hard clutch, clutch lever, clutch cable
rows.c: TVS manual: clutch lever free play 8–13 mm at the lever tip. Too little play can make the clutch slip and hard shifts/false neutrals; too much makes neutral and 1st gear hard to find. Adjust at the lever's barrel adjuster, and keep the cable lubed. A frayed or sticky cable should be replaced.

rows.t: Ronin spark plug type and gap
rows.k: spark plug, plug type, iridium, ngk, bosch, plug gap
rows.c: TVS manual: Bosch UR4KE, gap 0.8–0.9 mm, replace every 12,000 km or 1 year. Several RWB riders use the NGK iridium CR7EIX as an upgrade. A worn or wet plug causes hard starting and misfires.

rows.t: Ronin battery, fuses and lights
rows.k: battery, battery spec, 12v 6ah, fuse, fuse rating, headlight watt, abs fuse, ems fuse
rows.c: TVS manual: battery 12 V 6 Ah VRLA (maintenance-free). Charge it with a proper charger if it reads below 12.4 V. Fuses (side panel fuse box): ABS 20 A (dual-channel) or 15 A (single-channel), DC load 15 A, EMS 10 A, plus a main fuse; spare fuses are in the box. All lights are 12 V LED (headlamp 30 W/12 W).

rows.t: Ronin brake fluid and brakes
rows.k: brake fluid, brake oil, dot 4, dot 3, brake pads, disc size, abs
rows.c: Ronin brakes: 300 mm front disc (2-piston caliper) and 240 mm rear disc, with ABS (single-channel on Base, dual-channel from Base+). Brake fluid: TVS Girling DOT 3 or DOT 4 (don't mix types). Replace every 21,000 km or 2 years; check the level and pad thickness at every service. RWB riders usually see front pads last about 8,000–15,000 km.

rows.t: Ronin fuel tank, fuel gauge bars and DTE (distance to empty)
rows.k: fuel tank, reserve, fuel bars, low fuel light, dte, range, distance to empty, how far on reserve
rows.c: Tank: 14 L (TVS spec). TVS manual fuel gauge: 9 bars above about 10.3 L, 4 bars at about 6.1 L, 1 bar at about 3.2 L; the low-fuel light blinks at about 2.6 L and stays on at about 2 L. DTE (Mode button cycles ODO, Trip A, Trip B, DTE) shows only with 1–8 bars. Don't switch the ignition on with an almost empty tank (it can harm the fuel pump). RWB riders report about 25–35 km after the low-fuel warning; refill early.

rows.t: Ronin real-world mileage
rows.k: mileage, kmpl, fuel efficiency, average, claimed mileage, how much mileage
rows.c: TVS claims about 42 km/l. RWB riders usually see high 30s to mid 40s (city about 37–43, highway 40–47 km/l), depending on riding style, tyre pressure, load and petrol. Smooth throttle, steady 60–75 km/h, correct tyre pressure and a clean, lubed chain help most. Log every fill in the app's Mileage screen to know your real figure.

rows.t: Ronin riding modes, ABS and traction control
rows.k: rain mode, urban mode, ride mode, abs light, mode change error, ch err
rows.c: The Ronin has Rain and Urban modes. Change modes only with the throttle closed. If the bike detects a fault in the engine management (EMS) or ABS, it runs only in Urban mode after an ignition reset and shows "MODE CHANGE ERROR" (or "Ch Err" on the non-connected cluster): get it checked. The Top variant adds traction control. An ABS warning light that stays on after you ride off means ABS isn't working: ride gently and get it checked.

rows.t: Ronin side stand sensor: bike won't start
rows.k: side stand, won't start, no crank, kill switch, neutral, side stand indicator
rows.c: The Ronin won't start with the side stand down (it shows a side-stand indication). If it won't crank: kill switch on RUN, side stand fully up, in neutral or clutch pulled, battery OK. RWB riders say the side-stand sensor can get dirty or weak with time (mud, grease); cleaning it often fixes it, otherwise replace it at the service centre.

rows.t: Ronin ISG / engine malfunction (MIL) warning light
rows.k: isg light, check engine light, malfunction light, engine light, warning lamp, won't start isg, blue plug
rows.c: The Ronin uses an ISG (Integrated Starter Generator: silent starts, no separate starter motor). If the ISG or engine malfunction light stays ON, get it checked at TVS. RWB riders report two common causes: the blue ISG connector under the right side of the tank working loose (unplug, clean, plug back firmly), and a damaged sensor/magnet coil wire near the front sprocket (often after the chain slaps it). If it feels unsafe, stop and call TVS roadside help.

rows.t: Ronin false neutral and hard gear shifts
rows.k: false neutral, gear slipping, gear jumps, hard shift, neutral problem, gear sensor
rows.c: Riders report occasional false neutrals on the Ronin. What helps: correct clutch free play (8–13 mm), a clean and lubed gear-shift linkage and pivot, a clean front sprocket area (lube gunk builds up there), correct chain slack, and a firm, full shift with your boot. If it keeps happening or the gear indicator acts up, ask TVS to check the gear position sensor (some riders had it replaced under warranty).

rows.t: Ronin rattling noises and vibration
rows.k: rattle, noise, vibration, ticking, tick tick, sound, loose part
rows.c: Common Ronin rattles reported by RWB riders: a loose number plate or its holder, a chain that's too tight or dry, and loose panel/visor screws. A light "tik-tik" from the engine when warm is normal on the Ronin. New or loud knocking, grinding or a change in sound means get it checked. Buzz through the pegs above about 80 km/h is a known single-cylinder trait.

rows.t: Ronin water in the instrument cluster or electricals after rain/washing
rows.k: water in meter, fogged cluster, moisture console, washing damage, rain electrical
rows.c: Avoid pressure-washing the cluster, switches, spark plug cap and connectors. If moisture fogs the cluster, park it in sun/shade with the ignition off and let it dry; if water stays or it glitches, show it at TVS (it may be a warranty item). After washing, dry with compressed air or a blower and wait until the engine is cool before washing (RWB washing guide).

rows.t: Ronin engine heating in traffic
rows.k: overheating, engine heat, hot engine, heat on legs, traffic heat
rows.c: The Ronin is oil-cooled (it has an oil cooler, no radiator or coolant). It gets warm in long traffic jams, which is normal; most RWB riders don't find it a problem. Keep the oil fresh and at the right level, don't idle for very long, and switch off at long signals if you're comfortable. Real overheating signs (oil warning, power loss, smell, smoke) mean stop and get it checked.

rows.t: Ronin oil leak or seepage
rows.k: oil leak, oil seepage, drain bolt leak, oil mark, gasket
rows.c: Small oil marks are most often from the drain bolt (replace its washer at every oil change and tighten correctly, don't over-tighten) or the oil filter cover O-ring. Seepage from the cylinder head points to a gasket. Wipe it clean, ride, and check where fresh oil appears, then show the service centre. A real leak (drips, oil on the tyre) means don't ride far: oil on a tyre is dangerous.

rows.t: Ronin bike pulls to one side / handlebar not straight
rows.k: pulls left, pulls right, alignment, handle not straight, wheel alignment
rows.c: Some Ronin owners report the bike pulling to one side. Check tyre pressures first, then rear wheel alignment (both adjuster marks equal), chain adjusters, steering head bearing and a bent fork after a fall. Ask the service centre to check alignment with a proper procedure.

rows.t: Ronin vs Hunter 350 vs XSR 155: quick comparison
rows.k: compare, better bike, which to buy, ronin or hunter, ronin or xsr
rows.c: Ronin 225: light (159–160 kg), easy, comfy upright scrambler-ish ride, USD fork, slipper clutch, good mileage (high 30s–40s), 5 speeds. RE Hunter 350: heavier (about 181 kg), 349 cc thump, more torque, bigger service network. Yamaha XSR 155: lightest (137 kg), revvy liquid-cooled VVA engine, stiffer suspension, small 10 L tank. Test ride all; for rough Bengal roads and touring comfort the Ronin is a sweet spot.

rows.t: Ronin tyre upgrades and wider rear tyre
rows.k: tyre upgrade, better tyres, 140/70, wider tyre, best tyre for ronin, apollo tramplr, eurogrip, ceat, mrf
rows.c: Stock: TVS Eurogrip block-tread tyres. Popular RWB upgrades: Apollo Tramplr XR (dual-purpose, good in rain and mud), TVS Eurogrip Protorq/Roadhound, MRF and CEAT road tyres. Some riders fit a 140/70-17 rear; it looks beefier and can feel planted, but check clearance with the chain/swingarm, and the speedometer may read slightly differently. Always use tubeless tyres of the right load/speed rating, and replace a tyre at the wear-bar or around 5–6 years old (check the DOT date).

rows.t: Ronin popular accessories and mods
rows.k: accessories, mods, modification, crash guard, engine guard, saddle stay, top rack, visor, windscreen, mobile holder, usb charger
rows.c:
Popular with RWB riders: TVS official engine/leg guard (about ₹1,999) or Moto Torque crash guard, saddle stays and top rack for touring, tank bag (9–12 L), rackless saddle bags (22–46 L), TVS visor (looks more than wind protection), aux lights mounted low with the beam pointing down, a USB/Type-C charger (comes on newer variants), a navigation screen instead of a phone mount (phone mounts can damage phone camera OIS from vibration).
Not recommended by RWB riders: handlebar risers (can loosen), bar-end mirrors (break easily), headlight grills (hard to clean), loud aftermarket silencers (illegal and noisy).

rows.t: Ronin service cost (rough)
rows.k: service cost, service charge, how much service, paid service price, labour
rows.c: RWB riders report a regular paid service at a TVS centre around ₹1,800–3,000 (oil, filter, chain clean/lube, wash, labour); more when pads, tyres or a chain kit are replaced. Ask for the job card estimate before work starts and keep old parts if replaced. Prices vary by city and dealer.

rows.t: TVS customer care and roadside assistance
rows.k: tvs helpline, customer care number, roadside assistance, rsa, tvs toll free
rows.c: TVS customer care: 1800-258-7111 (toll free). For roadside help, check the RSA details in your TVS Connect app or warranty/RSA papers. In an emergency call 112, and use SOS in the RWB app.

rows.t: Buying a used Ronin: what to check
rows.k: second hand ronin, used ronin, pre-owned bike check, buy old ronin
rows.c: Check: service history and bills, odometer vs wear (pegs, levers, tyres), chain/sprockets, fork seals for oil, brake pads/discs, cold start (should start instantly), warning lights all go off, no smoke, clean gear shifts, straight frame/steering after a test ride, RC/insurance/PUC and the VIN/engine numbers matching the RC, and no pending challans. Use the RWB app's VRN check to see if it belonged to an RWB member.
